overview.bigIdea: Geometry is built from a few simple ideas: **points, lines, rays and angles**. An angle is really an **amount of turning** – and we measure that turn in degrees with a protractor.

ladder.a: A location, named with a capital letter
Two ends · no ends · one end
Vertex + two arms; size = amount of turn

overview.languagesTitle: Three things to do with an angle

languages.name: Name it
languages.text: ∠PQR – vertex letter always in the middle.

languages.name: Measure / draw it
languages.text: Protractor: centre on vertex, count from 0° on one arm.

plan.text: Lesson 1 and 2: definitions and naming – these are quick 1- and 2-mark answers.
Lesson 3: learn the five angle types with their degree ranges.
Lesson 4 with a real protractor: measure 5 angles and draw 80°, 160° and 135°.
Check knowledge quiz (protractor reading questions), revise after 1, 3, 7 days.

lessons.title: Point, line segment, line and ray
lessons.hook: Stretch a string tightly between two pins – that is a **line segment**, the shortest path between two points. Now imagine a torch beam starting at the torch and going on forever – that is a **ray**.

core.def: Shows an exact location. Named with a capital letter, e.g. P.
The shortest distance between points S and T. It has **two end points** and a fixed length.
A line segment extended **indefinitely on both sides**. No end points. Can also be named with one small letter, e.g. line m.
Starts at D and goes on **indefinitely in one direction** through P. The starting point is written first.

explain: Only a line segment can be measured with a ruler – a line and a ray go on forever.
Through one point you can draw countless lines; through two points there is **exactly one** line.

example.q: Name all the line segments, lines and rays: points A, B, C are on a straight line, with arrows at both ends of the line, and a ray starts at B going through C.
steps: Line segments: AB, BC, AC (each has two end points).
Line: AC (or AB, BC – the same line), extended both ways.
Ray: BC (starts at B, goes through C).
example.answer: Segments AB, BC, AC; line AC; ray BC.

mistakes: Writing ray DP as ray PD – the starting point must come first.
Saying a line has two end points.
lessons.tip: Use the right symbol-words: ‘line segment AB’, ‘ray AB’, ‘line AB’. Mixing them up loses the 1-mark answers.
lessons.memory: Segment: 2 ends · Ray: 1 end · Line: 0 ends.
examAsk: The shortest distance between two points is a …
How many lines pass through two points?
Name the rays/segments in a figure.

cards.q: How many end points does a ray have?

cards.a: No – it goes on forever both ways.

lessons.title: Angles: naming and comparing
lessons.hook: Open a door, turn a key, move the hands of a clock – each is a **turn**. When two rays start from the same point, the turn from one ray to the other is an **angle**.

core.def: Formed by two rays with a common starting point.
The common starting point of the two rays.
The two rays that form the angle.
∠POM or ∠MOP – the **vertex letter is always in the middle**.
The **amount of rotation** about the vertex needed to turn one arm onto the other. It does NOT depend on the length of the arms.

explain: To compare two angles, place one on top of the other with the vertices and one arm matching (superimposing) – the one whose other arm is further out is bigger.
A figure can hide several angles at one vertex: with rays TP, TQ, TR from T, the angles are ∠PTQ, ∠QTR and ∠PTR.

example.q: In the figure, rays TP, TQ and TR start at T. Name the two marked angles that both have arm TR. (Model paper Q24, 2 marks)
steps: The vertex is T, so T goes in the middle.
The angle between TR and TQ is ∠RTQ (or ∠QTR).
The angle between TR and TP is ∠RTP (or ∠PTR).

mistakes: Putting the vertex letter first or last (∠TRQ instead of ∠RTQ).
Thinking longer arms make a bigger angle.
lessons.tip: When a figure has three rays from one vertex, list every pair of rays – that gives all the angles (3 rays → 3 angles).
lessons.memory: Vertex in the middle! Size = turn, not arm length.
examAsk: Name the marked angles in a figure.
Identify the vertex and arms of ∠ABC.
Does the size change if the arms are extended?

cards.a: Amount of turn between its arms.

diagram.caption: ∠RTQ: vertex T, arms TR and TQ.

lessons.title: Special types of angles
lessons.hook: Stand facing the board and turn right round to face it again – a **full turn**, 360°. Turn to face the back of the class – a **half turn**, 180°, a straight angle. Turn to face the side wall – a **quarter turn**, 90°, a right angle.

core.def: Half turn = 180° (the arms make a straight line)
Quarter turn = 90°. Lines meeting at right angles are **perpendicular**.

explain: Why 360? A full turn was divided into 360 equal parts long ago; 360 divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 … which makes many angles whole numbers.
Clock angles: 12 hour marks share 360°, so each hour mark is 30°. At 3 o’clock the hands make 90°; at 6 o’clock, 180°.

steps: 180° is half a turn → straight angle.
90° is a quarter turn → right angle.

mistakes: Calling 90° acute or 180° obtuse – they are exactly right and straight.
Saying ‘perpendicular’ for any two crossing lines.
lessons.tip: Draw a quick number line 0 – 90 – 180 – 360 in the margin and place the angle on it. The type is instant.
lessons.memory: A-R-O-S-R: Acute < Right (90) < Obtuse < Straight (180) < Reflex < Full (360).
examAsk: Angle between clock hands at a given hour.
How many right angles make a straight angle / full turn?

diagram.caption: An obtuse angle of 130° – more than a right angle, less than a straight angle.

lessons.title: Measuring and drawing angles
lessons.hook: A protractor is simply a half-turn (180°) marked into degrees. The two number scales let you start counting from **either** arm – the whole skill is choosing the scale that starts at 0° on your arm.

core.def: Instrument to measure and draw angles in degrees.
Centre point on the **vertex**, base line along **one arm**.
Use the scale that reads **0°** on the arm lying on the base line.
If two rays read 65° and 115° on the same scale, the angle between them is 115° − 65° = 50°.
Draw a ray, put the centre on its end point, mark the degree from the 0° side, join.

explain: **Sense check:** decide first if the angle is acute or obtuse. If it looks acute but you read 150°, you used the wrong scale.
Angles on a straight line add up to 180°: if ∠AXB = 65°, then ∠BXE = 180° − 65° = 115°.

example.q: On the straight line AXE, rays XB and XC read 65° and 95° from A. Find ∠AXB, ∠BXC, ∠CXE and ∠BXE. (Model paper Q33, 3 marks)

mistakes: Starting from the wrong scale (reading 115° for a 65° angle).
Not placing the centre exactly on the vertex.
Forgetting to subtract when the angle is between two rays.
lessons.tip: In drawing questions (e.g. draw 80° and 160°), label the vertex, the arms and the degree clearly. Keep the protractor mark as a small dot before joining.
lessons.memory: Centre on vertex · base on arm · count from zero.
examAsk: Read angles from a protractor diagram.
Find the missing angle on a straight line.

cards.q: Where does the protractor centre go?
On a straight line, one angle is 65°. The other?

diagram.caption: Model paper Q33 style: read both rays from 0° at A.

formulas.name: Ray
formulas.f: 1 end point, goes on in one direction

formulas.name: Straight line
formulas.f: angles on a line add to 180°

revision: A point marks a location; name it with a capital letter.
Line segment: shortest distance between two points, two end points. Line: no end points. Ray: one starting point.
Name rays with the starting point first (ray DP starts at D).
An angle = two rays from a common point; vertex = common point; arms = the rays.
Name an angle with the vertex in the middle: ∠POM = ∠MOP.
Size of an angle = amount of rotation; arm length does not matter.
Full turn 360°, straight angle 180°, right angle 90°.
Perpendicular lines meet at right angles.
Protractor: centre on vertex, base line on one arm, read from the 0° on that arm.
Angle between two rays = difference of their readings; angles on a straight line add to 180°.

sections.title: Protractor questions · 4 checks
items: Read from the scale that shows 0° on that arm.
Sense check: acute or obtuse? Does the number match?

sections.title: Naming and classifying
items: Vertex letter in the middle every time.
List every pair of rays at a vertex to find all angles.

sections.title: Answer writing
items: Write the rule or definition in one line first, then apply it – rule lines earn marks even if the arithmetic slips.
Show every step on its own line (for example each division in a prime factorisation or each Kaprekar round).
Underline or box the final answer and write the unit (°, students, books) where there is one.
For ‘Give reason / Justify’ questions: state the rule, then show that the number or figure fits (or does not fit) it.

checklist: I can tell a line, line segment and ray apart and name them correctly.
I can name angles with the vertex in the middle.
I know the five angle types and their ranges.
I can find clock-hand angles at whole hours.
I can read two rays on a protractor and subtract.
I can draw any angle up to 180° accurately.

method: Built on proven learning methods: see it as a picture first, understand why it works, learn from worked examples, then test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
